title: Monthly Decision Maker Panel data - April 2026
summary: UK businesses surveyed in April 2026 reported year-ahead own-price inflation expectations rising to 3.8% from 3.5% in March, with the single-month data showing a sharper increase from 3.4% to 4.4% between February and April, indicating firms are adjusting expectations in response to recent energy price increases. CPI inflation expectations also rose to 3.5% for year-ahead and 2.8% for three-year ahead. Employment conditions are weakening with realized annual employment growth at -0.4% and expectations at 0.0%.
key_points: Year-ahead own-price inflation expectation: 3.8% in April, up 0.3 percentage points from March (single-month data shows 3.4% to 4.4% jump Feb-Apr)
Year-ahead CPI inflation expectations rose to 3.5% in April, up from 3.1% in March (single-month: 3.0% to 4.0%)
Three-year ahead CPI inflation expectations: 2.8%, up 0.1 percentage points from March
Realized annual own-price growth was 3.7% in the three months to April, unchanged from March
Wage growth: realized at 4.3% (unchanged), expected year-ahead at 3.4% (down from 3.5%)
Employment: realized annual growth at -0.4%, expectations for next year at 0.0% (both weakened)
Energy shock adjustments: 64% of firms expect to increase prices, 68% expect lower profit margins, 26% expect higher wages
why_it_matters: The DMP survey provides real-time insight into UK business pricing and employment intentions, serving as an early indicator of inflationary pressures and economic momentum. The sharp upward shift in inflation expectations—especially the single-month move to 4.4%—suggests energy price increases are rapidly feeding through to business pricing behavior. This data iswatched by the Bank of England as it informs the MPC's assessment of domestic price and wage dynamics beyond official statistics.
macro_context: The survey shows firms adjusting inflation expectations upward in response to energy price shocks, with price intentions rising more sharply than headline CPI expectations. Employment expectations have turned negative, suggesting labor market cooling. The combination of higher expected prices and weaker employment outlook creates a challenging backdrop for the MPC—potentially stagflationary signals at a time when energy costs are pressuring margins.

notes: Survey data from 2,030 UK CFOs conducted 2-17 April 2026. Published by Bank of England in collaboration with King's College London and University of Nottingham. The single-month data shows more dramatic shifts than the quarterly aggregates—year-ahead own-price expectations jumped from 3.4% to 4.4% between February and April, and CPI expectations from 3.0% to 4.0%. This may indicate firms are forward-looking and reacting to energy price shocks faster than aggregate data would suggest. Employment expectations turning negative (0.0%) for the first time in recent comparisons suggests businesses are preparing for headwinds. Not a policy decision or rate announcement, but highly relevant for macro catalyst analysis as it captures business sentiment and pricing intentions ahead of official data.
